Database searches yielded 2,767 records, and backward citation searching identified one additional report. <sentence_start/>Overall, 47 reports representing 38 study units were included.
Study and Report Characteristics

The 47 included reports, published between 1993 and 2026, covered randomized trials, controlled and uncontrolled non-randomized intervention studies, longitudinal and cross-sectional observational studies, retrospective administrative cohorts, a linked qualitative companion report on barriers and advice, and small case series. <sentence_start/>Sample sizes ranged from two participants in a perioperative case series to several hundred participants in national surveys and administrative cohorts. <sentence_start/>Most training studies in community settings enrolled selected adults with stable, mild-to-moderate generalized MG. <sentence_start/>Evidence for ocular MG, severe or unstable disease, major bulbar or respiratory compromise, and substantial cardiopulmonary comorbidity was sparse.

Linking related reports reduced the 47 included reports to 38 study units. <sentence_start/>Reports were grouped using explicit trial links, ethics identifiers, recruitment sites and dates, characteristics of individual participants or groups, intervention methods, and exact source statements. <sentence_start/>Confirmed links were distinguished from possible overlap. <sentence_start/>Denominators from each report were retained, and uncertain relationships were not classified as either wholly independent or fully overlapping.

Six publications from the Surabaya Centre were assigned to three trial families. <sentence_start/>Four reports shared ethics approval (0601/KEPK/II/2023), the same setting, closely similar intervention and comparator programmes, and substantially overlapping dates; they were treated as one apparent parent trial, although their randomized and analysed denominators were irreconcilable [<citation rid="REF17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.52225/narra.v4i3.844" pmcid="PMC11731934" pmid="39816114" count="1">17</citation>,<citation rid="REF39" ref-type="bibr" count="1">39</citation>-<citation rid="REF41" ref-type="bibr" count="1">41</citation>].

Kartika et al. and Anggarini et al. had different ethics approvals and nonidentical flows, so they were not formally merged [<citation rid="REF16" ref-type="bibr" count="1">16</citation>,<citation rid="REF42" ref-type="bibr" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, their final intervention groups each contained nine participants with the same reported mean age and standard deviation (47.78 ± 5.36 years) and the same sex distribution (two men and seven women) [<citation rid="REF16" ref-type="bibr" count="1">16</citation>,<citation rid="REF42" ref-type="bibr" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Partial or substantial participant overlap is therefore probable but could not be confirmed. <sentence_start/>The synthesis treats them as separate trial components with an explicit non-independence warning.

Two other groups of publications were explicitly linked. <sentence_start/>The Benefits and Tolerance of Exercise in Myasthenia Gravis (MGEX) trial produced an accelerometry analysis conducted before randomization and a randomized home rowing report [<citation rid="REF30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JND-210637" pmid="33843693" count="1">30</citation>,<citation rid="REF43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2021.05.002" pmid="34304969" count="1">43</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The Rest or 30-Min Walk as Exercise Intervention (RESTOREX) trial produced a primary randomized report and a linked biomarker and clinical subanalysis of 15 participants [<citation rid="REF28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000513668" pmid="33839731" count="1">28</citation>,<citation rid="REF29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12035-023-03247-5" pmid="36781738" count="1">29</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The 12 healthy controls in the latter provided only baseline biomarker comparisons and were not treated as a second comparative MG study [<citation rid="REF28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000513668" pmid="33839731" count="1">28</citation>,<citation rid="REF29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12035-023-03247-5" pmid="36781738" count="1">29</citation>].

Participant overlap also affected publications on respiratory training and reports from Sweden, Denmark, and Australia. <sentence_start/>Nine of the 10 participants in Rassler et al. (2011) could be matched directly to participants labelled TG1-TG9 in the later Freitag cohort. <sentence_start/>Five had already participated in the 2007 episode, and the final Freitag cohort contained seven previous participants, including one who later entered as a control [<citation rid="REF21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.rmed.2018.09.001" pmid="30366587" count="1">21</citation>,<citation rid="REF44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2007.01.001" pmid="17336068" count="1">44</citation>,<citation rid="REF45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4061/2011/808607" pmcid="PMC3159986" pmid="21869926" count="1">45</citation>].

O'Connor et al. pooled the two complete baseline samples from the Uppsala (n = 14) and Jönköping (n = 13) intervention cohorts; the pooled sample was therefore not counted as a third cohort [<citation rid="REF31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JND-180355" pmid="30452423" count="1">31</citation>,<citation rid="REF46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.25493" pmid="27935072" count="1">46</citation>,<citation rid="REF47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MD.0000000000011510" pmcid="PMC6081147" pmid="30075515" count="1">47</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The Swedish survey reports reused the same 40 Jönköping respondents, and possible overlap between that survey sample and the 13-person Jönköping exercise cohort could not be reconstructed [<citation rid="REF46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.25493" pmid="27935072" count="1">46</citation>,<citation rid="REF48" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/ane.13017" pmid="30155967" count="1">48</citation>,<citation rid="REF49" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/brb3.653" pmcid="PMC5390836" pmid="28413704" count="1">49</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Punga et al. recruited mainly from the earlier Uppsala cohort, but the exact number who had participated previously was not reported [<citation rid="REF26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2023.02.009" pmid="36931100" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="REF47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MD.0000000000011510" pmcid="PMC6081147" pmid="30075515" count="1">47</citation>].

Andersen and Vissing reanalysed the Danish national survey and additionally described a 69-patient clinic component; participant overlap between these components was not reported [<citation rid="REF50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2021.05.007" pmid="34303571" count="1">50</citation>,<citation rid="REF51" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JND-210693" pmid="34334414" count="1">51</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The Alsop qualitative report selected 10 participants from the earlier 85-person survey project [<citation rid="REF52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JND-210722" pmid="34633330" count="1">52</citation>,<citation rid="REF53" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/09638288.2024.2338877" pmid="38613411" count="1">53</citation>], and Thomsen et al. followed participants from two earlier Vinge baseline cohorts rather than creating a new baseline population [<citation rid="REF54" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2022.02.007" pmid="35279342" count="1">54</citation>].
Risk of Bias Across the Evidence Base

Risk of bias was a dominant limitation across all evidence streams. <sentence_start/>Judgments for randomized studies differed by result: patient-reported outcomes from participants who knew their allocation, outcomes with substantial missing data, and results affected by selective reporting were commonly at high risk, whereas some objective results had some concerns. <sentence_start/>No certainty rating for randomized evidence was upgraded on the basis of favourable uncontrolled or observational findings. <sentence_start/>Among the four ROBINS-I assessments, Otaka, Hsu, and the Leipzig RMET result after long-term follow-up were at critical overall risk of bias; Ambrogi's comparison of length of stay among selected matched completers remained at serious risk.

The principal concerns were confounding and reverse causality, selection of analysed participants, definition of exposure after baseline, attrition related to prognosis, measurements influenced by participant effort, invalid or absent comparative analyses, and selective reporting. <sentence_start/>Every efficacy assessment from an uncontrolled single-group study was judged to have a high concern because neither a concurrent control nor an adequate repeated baseline separated the intervention from natural history, regression to the mean, additional care, or time effects. <sentence_start/>Most analyses of habitual activity were cross-sectional or otherwise vulnerable to self-reported exposure, attrition, limited adjustment, uncertain causal direction, selective availability of device data, dependence among observations, and internally inconsistent source data. <sentence_start/>Linked secondary analyses were appraised according to their actual design.
Habitual Physical Activity, Sedentary Behaviour, and Barriers

Studies using accelerometers or questionnaires reported heterogeneous activity patterns in selected MG samples. <sentence_start/>These included substantial variation between participants in activity measured by devices and differences in whether physical activity and sedentary behaviour thresholds were met [<citation rid="REF30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JND-210637" pmid="33843693" count="1">30</citation>,<citation rid="REF31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JND-180355" pmid="30452423" count="1">31</citation>,<citation rid="REF52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JND-210722" pmid="34633330" count="1">52</citation>,<citation rid="REF55" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.28282" pmcid="PMC11632566" pmid="39473433" count="1">55</citation>,<citation rid="REF56" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fneur.2023.1144183" pmcid="PMC10427188" pmid="37588667" count="1">56</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Adjusted inverse associations between self-reported activity and fatigue were reported in Danish national and Dutch registry surveys [<citation rid="REF50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2021.05.007" pmid="34303571" count="1">50</citation>,<citation rid="REF57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2021.04.002" pmid="34034925" count="1">57</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Earlier reports from Sweden and Estonia compared participants with MG with matched controls or compared national cohorts. <sentence_start/>They reported differences in activity patterns but did not estimate an adjusted association within the MG population between activity and fatigue or another patient-reported outcome [<citation rid="REF48" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/ane.13017" pmid="30155967" count="1">48</citation>,<citation rid="REF49" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/brb3.653" pmcid="PMC5390836" pmid="28413704" count="1">49</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Grohar-Murray et al. reported no significant overall relationship between fatigue scores and self-care actions. <sentence_start/>Among 36 respondents who used low-impact aerobic exercise, 25 considered it helpful, and 11 did not; fatigue scores did not differ significantly by perceived helpfulness [<citation rid="REF58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/01376517-199806000-00007" pmid="9689611" count="1">58</citation>].

Cross-sectional studies cannot establish direction. <sentence_start/>People with less fatigue, lower MG severity, fewer comorbidities, better mobility, or more favourable social circumstances may be more able to exercise. <sentence_start/>In the 12-week Dimmick cohort, 30 participants were enrolled, but only 16 had sufficient data for the final analyses. <sentence_start/>Models centred on the cohort mean did not isolate change within each participant. <sentence_start/>They associated fewer steps, less moderate-to-vigorous and light activity, and more inactivity with worse fatigue or MG symptom ratings on the same day. <sentence_start/>In models scaled within each participant, the only retained daily behavioural association was between more moderate-to-vigorous activity and less fatigue; no daily activity or sleep variable was retained for symptom ratings. <sentence_start/>Individual estimates varied in direction, and one reported dispersion value and two reported confidence intervals were internally implausible [<citation rid="REF55" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.28282" pmcid="PMC11632566" pmid="39473433" count="1">55</citation>].

A decentralized smartphone study related optional platform-derived step counts to MG-ADL scores and self-reported exacerbation status recorded on the same day. <sentence_start/>Only 26 participants contributed data to the analysis relating step count to MG-ADL, and 14 to the analysis relating exacerbation status to step count. <sentence_start/>These analyses did not account for repeated observations within participants; harmonization across devices or platforms, criteria for wear time, and thresholds for completeness of step data were not reported. <sentence_start/>The record listed audiovisual symptom recording as a primary outcome and MG-specific quality of life as a secondary outcome; neither was reported in the article [<citation rid="REF12" ref-type="bibr" count="1">12</citation>,<citation rid="REF56" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fneur.2023.1144183" pmcid="PMC10427188" pmid="37588667" count="1">56</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Over a mean follow-up of 4.6 years, Thomsen et al. found no change in the self-reported Physical Activity Scale score among participants with MG (p = 0.393) [<citation rid="REF54" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2022.02.007" pmid="35279342" count="1">54</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Physical Activity Scale scores did not differ significantly between the MG and control groups at either visit.

Unadjusted Pearson analyses among completers found a weak correlation between changes in activity and shoulder strength (r = 0.324, p = 0.01). <sentence_start/>Changes in activity did not correlate with changes in knee strength, 400-m walk performance, or the 30-second sit-to-stand test; the correlation with change in ankle strength was not reported [<citation rid="REF54" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2022.02.007" pmid="35279342" count="1">54</citation>].

The Alsop survey adjusted only for age, body mass index, and disease duration. <sentence_start/>Meeting its self-reported threshold of at least 500 metabolic equivalent minutes per week was associated with lower fatigue, better MG-specific quality of life, less walking limitation, and greater balance confidence. <sentence_start/>Sedentary time reported as less than 10 versus at least 10 hours per day was not associated with any of these outcomes. <sentence_start/>In the joint analysis, participants with insufficient activity and high sedentary time had greater fatigue, poorer MG-specific quality of life, more walking limitation, and lower balance confidence than the reference group with sufficient activity and less sedentary time. <sentence_start/>Participants with insufficient activity and less sedentary time had greater fatigue, poorer MG-specific quality of life, and more walking limitation than the reference group, but balance confidence did not differ. <sentence_start/>Several reported estimates contained incompatible coefficients, confidence intervals, or p-values, so those exact estimates were not interpreted [<citation rid="REF52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JND-210722" pmid="34633330" count="1">52</citation>].

In the Danish registry survey, each one-category increase in the modified Saltin-Grimby Physical Activity Level Scale was associated, after multivariable adjustment of complete cases, with lower scores in all five Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory domains. <sentence_start/>In the sensitivity analysis restricted to participants who were treated and regularly followed by a neurologist, the estimate for mental fatigue was null while the other four associations remained. <sentence_start/>Andersen and Vissing subsequently reanalysed 691 complete cases from the same survey of 779 respondents using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire and also reported a separate clinic accelerometer sample of 69 patients [<citation rid="REF50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2021.05.007" pmid="34303571" count="1">50</citation>,<citation rid="REF51" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JND-210693" pmid="34334414" count="1">51</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In the cross-sectional registry survey by Ruiter et al., one or more sessions of strenuous activity per week were associated with lower fatigue scores than no strenuous activity in the adjusted model of 397 participants. <sentence_start/>No category of daily moderate activity was associated with fatigue. <sentence_start/>The model included demographic and clinical variables, depressive symptoms, sleep quality, autoimmune comorbidity, and both activity measures, but not MG treatment [<citation rid="REF57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2021.04.002" pmid="34034925" count="1">57</citation>].

Glaubitz et al. reported unadjusted inverse Spearman correlations of a study-specific metabolic-equivalent score with the Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis (QMG) score (r = -0.255, p = 0.019) and MG-ADL (r = -0.316, p = 0.004). <sentence_start/>No validation of the questionnaire was reported, and no treatment adjustment was made despite frequent corticosteroid, other immunosuppressive, and intravenous immunoglobulin use. <sentence_start/>Some quantities in the Glaubitz et al. report were labelled as steps per day. <sentence_start/>However, the questionnaire asked for self-reported daily walking distance in metres, optionally informed by a tracker, and did not report a conversion from metres to steps [<citation rid="REF59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12883-025-04590-x" pmcid="PMC12822234" pmid="41408204" count="1">59</citation>].

In qualitative interviews with 10 Australian adults with generalized MG, participants described fatigue, muscle weakness related to activity, and pain as barriers to physical activity, although the relation of pain to MG itself was uncertain. <sentence_start/>Effective medical management, social support, pacing and rest strategies, and perceived benefits to general health or MG facilitated activity, whereas professional advice was often considered inadequate or poorly tailored to MG [<citation rid="REF53" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/09638288.2024.2338877" pmid="38613411" count="1">53</citation>].

In a French online survey, perceived barriers included health or symptoms, lack of supervision by an MG specialist, fear of adverse disease or symptom consequences, weather, insufficient exercise knowledge, low motivation, time, company, and practical access. <sentence_start/>Reported facilitators included expected or experienced health and symptom benefits, specialist supervision or coaching, exercise information, practical access or affordability, company, and support from family or healthcare professionals [<citation rid="REF60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/22143602261463887" pmcid="PMC13439003" pmid="42348774" count="1">60</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Birnbaum et al. classified 244 of 455 participants (53.6%) as exercisers and 211 (46.4%) as non-exercisers; the abstract reported 54% and 47%, whereas one sentence in the Results reversed the group proportions. <sentence_start/>The internally consistent counts of 244 and 211 were therefore retained. <sentence_start/>As these data were self-reported and cross-sectional, and the survey comparisons were univariate, they describe perceived determinants and associations rather than effects of prescribing exercise.
Structured Exercise in Selected Community-Dwelling or Outpatient Adults

Controlled trials produced mixed findings across heterogeneous primary outcomes. <sentence_start/>DIG-MG randomized 81 participants; prespecified omnibus tests were null for MG-ADL and the Fatigue Severity Scale, and a nominal pairwise MG-ADL difference favoured passive monitoring rather than physical activity coaching [<citation rid="REF61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.70234" pmid="41999078" count="1">61</citation>]. <sentence_start/>MGEX randomized 43 participants; home rowing did not improve the prespecified primary MG-specific quality of life outcome at month six, and nominal findings for MG-ADL and six-minute walk distance at month six were not sustained at month nine [<citation rid="REF43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2021.05.002" pmid="34304969" count="1">43</citation>]. <sentence_start/>RESTOREX randomized 40 participants and analysed 38 completers.

The published MGQOL15 responder result, defined as improvement of more than 50%, favoured walking over rest. <sentence_start/>However, registration followed the trial; the sample size calculation addressed continuous change, multiple outcomes, time points, and responder thresholds were available, and the linked 15-person report could not be reconciled with the parent responder counts [<citation rid="REF13" ref-type="bibr" count="1">13</citation>,<citation rid="REF28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000513668" pmid="33839731" count="1">28</citation>,<citation rid="REF29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12035-023-03247-5" pmid="36781738" count="1">29</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The linked RESTOREX biomarker report retained only a selected uncontrolled walking group subset; healthy controls supplied baseline biology rather than a controlled exercise effect. <sentence_start/>Rahbek et al. compared resistance with aerobic training rather than exercise with usual care and analysed only 12 of 15 randomized participants [<citation rid="REF62" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.25552" pmid="28085204" count="1">62</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These results do not establish a consistent patient-centred benefit of structured exercise.

The Surabaya programme reported walking, fatigue, MG-ADL, disease severity, depression, pulmonary outcomes, and outcomes measured by surface electromyography across six publications [<citation rid="REF16" ref-type="bibr" count="1">16</citation>,<citation rid="REF17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.52225/narra.v4i3.844" pmcid="PMC11731934" pmid="39816114" count="1">17</citation>,<citation rid="REF39" ref-type="bibr" count="1">39</citation>-<citation rid="REF42" ref-type="bibr" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Four later reports were linked as one apparent ethics-0601 trial family, while Kartika and Anggarini were retained as separate components with probable but unconfirmed participant overlap. <sentence_start/>Positive findings frequently arose from analyses limited to completers, tests of change within groups, or endpoints measured after treatment rather than clearly reported comparisons of randomized groups.

Kartika's Fatigue Severity Scale data were inconsistent. <sentence_start/>Anggarini excluded five of 23 randomized participants and reported ambiguous pooled deltas. <sentence_start/>Amalina emphasized favourable endpoints despite stating that changes did not differ significantly between groups. <sentence_start/>Deliana et al. did not adequately describe normalization or processing of surface electromyography or assessor blinding [<citation rid="REF39" ref-type="bibr" count="1">39</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Small samples, attrition, unblinded assessment, effort-dependent or patient-reported outcomes, multiple publications presenting separate outcomes, unresolved cohort independence, and irreconcilable denominators produced high risk of bias for all principal Surabaya efficacy results.

Small uncontrolled programmes and case series reported selected improvements within participants. <sentence_start/>Without concurrent controls, however, these findings could not distinguish an intervention effect from natural fluctuation, regression to the mean, learning from repeated testing, additional care, or volunteer selection [<citation rid="REF26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2023.02.009" pmid="36931100" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="REF27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.24054" pmid="23966018" count="1">27</citation>,<citation rid="REF46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.25493" pmid="27935072" count="1">46</citation>,<citation rid="REF47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MD.0000000000011510" pmcid="PMC6081147" pmid="30075515" count="1">47</citation>,<citation rid="REF63" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/jcm10174031" pmcid="PMC8432538" pmid="34501479" count="1">63</citation>,<citation rid="REF64" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JND-170299" pmid="29889078" count="1">64</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In Chang et al., 35 participants entered and 34 completed. <sentence_start/>Participants chose their weekly exercise dose, and two groups of 17 were formed after the analysis at the median of 56.3 minutes per week; this was not a randomized comparison of exercise dose [<citation rid="REF63" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/jcm10174031" pmcid="PMC8432538" pmid="34501479" count="1">63</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Farrugia et al. enrolled 10 participants in a combined physical and psychological fatigue management programme and analysed nine after baseline. <sentence_start/>Only the Visual Analogue Fatigue Scale improved during treatment, and the improvement was not sustained [<citation rid="REF64" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JND-170299" pmid="29889078" count="1">64</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Punga et al. analysed seven completers recruited mainly from the earlier Westerberg Uppsala study, although the exact number reused was not reported [<citation rid="REF26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2023.02.009" pmid="36931100" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="REF47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MD.0000000000011510" pmcid="PMC6081147" pmid="30075515" count="1">47</citation>].

The Westerberg Uppsala cohort (14 entered and 11 completed) and Jönköping cohort (13 entered and 10 completed) were separate; O'Connor et al. later pooled baseline accelerometry from all 14 and 13 entrants, respectively [<citation rid="REF31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JND-180355" pmid="30452423" count="1">31</citation>,<citation rid="REF46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.25493" pmid="27935072" count="1">46</citation>,<citation rid="REF47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MD.0000000000011510" pmcid="PMC6081147" pmid="30075515" count="1">47</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Wong et al. enrolled seven participants in an individualized balance training case series and analysed six completers [<citation rid="REF27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.24054" pmid="23966018" count="1">27</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In Lohi et al. (n = 11), body side rather than participants was randomized: one arm and the contralateral leg were trained, with the opposite limbs serving as controls. <sentence_start/>Possible cross-education and a largely unachievable elbow-extension prescription limited inference from this limb-level design [<citation rid="REF65" ref-type="bibr" pmid="8239958" count="1">65</citation>].

The acute experiment with rhythmic auditory stimulation randomized the order of stimulated and standard six-minute walk tests within participants, not the cueing dose. <sentence_start/>The first 18 participants received stimulation at 100% of cadence, and the next 30 received 110% after interim observations. <sentence_start/>In the sequential cohort tested at 110%, stimulation increased six-minute walk distance by 8.3 m (95% confidence interval: 1.82-14.78; p = 0.01). <sentence_start/>This small effect of gait cueing, observed during a single visit, was of uncertain clinical importance and did not represent longitudinal conditioning [<citation rid="REF66" ref-type="bibr" count="1">66</citation>].
Respiratory Muscle Training

Studies of respiratory muscle training evaluated inspiratory training with a pressure threshold, combined inspiratory and expiratory training, and endurance training with normocapnic hyperpnoea at widely varying doses. <sentence_start/>In Fregonezi et al. (n = 27), between-group results favoured training for maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures. <sentence_start/>The full report, however, showed no significant difference between groups in respiratory endurance, only a change in MVV within the training group, and no meaningful benefit in spirometry or lung volumes. <sentence_start/>Sequence generation and concealment were unreported, withdrawal timing was unclear, effort influenced testing, adherence was unquantified, and the isolated favourable result for the role-physical domain of SF-36 was selected from nine domains [<citation rid="REF67" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1378/chest.128.3.1524" pmid="16162753" count="1">67</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Hsu et al. compared volunteers undertaking training with matched patients unwilling to train [<citation rid="REF22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2020/2923907" pmcid="PMC7114765" pmid="32280685" count="1">22</citation>].

The prescribed programme differed between sections, and information on adherence and medication changes was unavailable. <sentence_start/>The paper presented separate tests before and after treatment within each group rather than a valid comparison of changes between groups or a group-by-time interaction. <sentence_start/>A comparative causal effect was therefore not reliably estimable [<citation rid="REF22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2020/2923907" pmcid="PMC7114765" pmid="32280685" count="1">22</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Weiner et al. reported uncontrolled changes by severity group. <sentence_start/>Values for inspiratory pressure in the severe group duplicated forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) values; respiratory endurance in the severe group and dyspnoea in the moderate group were also reported inconsistently, so their exact magnitudes were unusable [<citation rid="REF68" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1017/s0317167100034077" pmid="9706726" count="1">68</citation>].

The Leipzig series comprised a selected short-term uncontrolled episode and a later long-term programme in which allocation depended on participant preference. <sentence_start/>Nine of 10 participants in the 2011 preliminary report mapped directly to participants labelled TG1-TG9 in the final report, seven final participants had received training in 2007, and one previously trained participant later entered as a control [<citation rid="REF21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.rmed.2018.09.001" pmid="30366587" count="1">21</citation>,<citation rid="REF44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2007.01.001" pmid="17336068" count="1">44</citation>,<citation rid="REF45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4061/2011/808607" pmcid="PMC3159986" pmid="21869926" count="1">45</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Only 10 of 20 selected patients entered the short-term episode.

In the long-term programme, allocation depended on willingness, motivation, available time, and previous experience. <sentence_start/>Only 12 of 18 trainees and five of six controls completed 13 months. <sentence_start/>Medication, training, and measurement timing were modified around illness, and respiratory endurance testing required maximal effort and active encouragement. <sentence_start/>The available result was a comparison of observed data from completers rather than an effect of assignment and was at critical risk of bias. <sentence_start/>Favourable signals for respiratory strength or endurance therefore remain very uncertain and are not independent replications across these overlapping reports.
Perioperative Rehabilitation and Rehabilitation After Crisis or Hospitalization

These studies addressed surgical recovery rather than chronic MG disease modification. <sentence_start/>Chen et al. reported a trial of 80 participants conducted around thymectomy, but the sequence and concealment methods, participant flow from screening, adherence, medication changes, and assessor blinding were not described. <sentence_start/>Hospital stay was listed as an outcome, but no result was reported. <sentence_start/>More importantly, many reported p-values comparing groups for baseline variables, postoperative pulmonary function, and early ADL were incompatible with the published means, standard deviations, and group sizes; the reported day 1 and day 3 ADL standard deviations were also inconsistent. <sentence_start/>It is therefore not possible to determine whether the means, dispersions, p-values, or analysis denominators are correct. <sentence_start/>Six-minute walk distance was null, and exact pulmonary and ADL inference remains unreconciled [<citation rid="REF69" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13019-023-02283-5" pmcid="PMC10127428" pmid="37095505" count="1">69</citation>].

Ambrogi and Mineo selected 17 of 44 rehabilitation completers and matched them to 17 historical controls who underwent surgery between 1999 and 2004. <sentence_start/>Reported categorical p-values for admission to intensive care, major morbidity, and improvement at one year were not reproducible from the published counts; the analysis of time to remission excluded participants who never achieved remission rather than censoring them. <sentence_start/>Only the comparison of length of stay among matched completers was retained as contextual evidence at serious risk of bias, not as a randomized or contemporaneous effect [<citation rid="REF20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/PHM.0000000000000538" pmid="28099277" count="1">20</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Polastri et al. supplied only two uncomplicated early postoperative cases and reported a dyspnoea value above the stated scale maximum [<citation rid="REF70" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28604379" count="1">70</citation>].

Otaka et al. analysed 473 hospitalizations following myasthenic crisis, although the abstract reported 437. <sentence_start/>Exposure was the accumulated number of billed rehabilitation units after ventilator weaning, not assignment at a common baseline. <sentence_start/>Recovery speed could therefore determine subsequent dose while also defining the outcome. <sentence_start/>The higher-intensity group was older and more impaired, with higher rates of tracheotomy and steroid pulse therapy, longer pre-index ventilation, and worse initial ADL. <sentence_start/>The conventional adjusted hazard ratio was 0.69 (95% confidence interval: 0.48-0.99), whereas inverse-probability weighting gave 0.79 (0.56-1.12). <sentence_start/>The result was at critical risk of bias and cannot establish that greater rehabilitation intensity delayed recovery [<citation rid="REF23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jns.2022.120280" pmid="35594695" count="1">23</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Chang et al. randomized 60 recently discharged adults and analysed 54 complete cases [<citation rid="REF71" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12890-025-03733-7" pmcid="PMC12107784" pmid="40426137" count="1">71</citation>].

The retrospectively registered primary comparison between groups for change in maximal inspiratory pressure was null (p = 0.18) [<citation rid="REF14" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>,<citation rid="REF71" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12890-025-03733-7" pmcid="PMC12107784" pmid="40426137" count="1">71</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Internally consistent secondary results favoured maximal expiratory pressure, six-minute walk distance, FEV1, and FVC. <sentence_start/>However, registration occurred almost six years after the trial, six randomized participants were excluded, reported Borg score and percent predicted FEV1 values were internally inconsistent, and the published effect size estimates and purported minimal clinically important differences could not be verified. <sentence_start/>Positive secondary findings were therefore at high risk of bias and could not override the null primary result [<citation rid="REF14" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>,<citation rid="REF71" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12890-025-03733-7" pmcid="PMC12107784" pmid="40426137" count="1">71</citation>].
Juvenile Myasthenia Gravis

One active comparator trial with blinded assessors randomized 30 stable adolescents to treadmill training with partial body weight support added to a substantial supervised physiotherapy programme or to the same physiotherapy alone [<citation rid="REF72" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/medicina58030374" pmcid="PMC8955821" pmid="35334548" count="1">72</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Sequence generation, CleanWeb allocation, blinded assessment, complete follow-up, unchanged medication and activity, and approximately 98% attendance were strengths. <sentence_start/>However, the University Hospital Medical Information Network (UMIN) registry and publication differed in age range, treatment duration, and blinding description; registered outcomes from repetitive nerve stimulation and MGQOL15 were not reported, while PedsQL fatigue and total scores were substituted [<citation rid="REF15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/medicina58030374" pmcid="PMC8955821" pmid="35334548" count="1">15</citation>,<citation rid="REF72" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/medicina58030374" pmcid="PMC8955821" pmid="35334548" count="1">72</citation>].

Spirometry, strength, and walking were influenced by effort; participants knew assignment, many outcomes were tested, confidence intervals were absent, and several reported standard deviations were implausibly small and could not be verified as SD rather than another dispersion measure. <sentence_start/>The trial suggests a possible incremental benefit from treadmill training but does not support a broad conclusion about the efficacy of juvenile rehabilitation
Disease Stability, Medication, and Pyridostigmine Timing

Stability definitions varied across studies. <sentence_start/>MGEX and Mohamed et al. required at least six months of stability. <sentence_start/>The RESTOREX parent report required three months, whereas its linked biomarker report required one month. <sentence_start/>Ceren et al. excluded recent crisis or a change in treatment dose within one month, and Fregonezi et al. excluded crisis within two months. <sentence_start/>Chang et al. excluded medication adjustment, unstable symptoms, intravenous immunoglobulin, or plasma exchange within six months [<citation rid="REF28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000513668" pmid="33839731" count="1">28</citation>,<citation rid="REF29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12035-023-03247-5" pmid="36781738" count="1">29</citation>,<citation rid="REF43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2021.05.002" pmid="34304969" count="1">43</citation>,<citation rid="REF63" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/jcm10174031" pmcid="PMC8432538" pmid="34501479" count="1">63</citation>,<citation rid="REF67" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1378/chest.128.3.1524" pmid="16162753" count="1">67</citation>,<citation rid="REF72" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/medicina58030374" pmcid="PMC8955821" pmid="35334548" count="1">72</citation>,<citation rid="REF73" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/09638288.2021.2022221" pmid="34978954" count="1">73</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Reports using only the terms controlled, stable, optimized, or outpatient were rated unclear.

MG treatment generally continued, but changes and concurrent immunotherapy were incompletely reported. <sentence_start/>Mohamed et al., Fregonezi et al., and Wong et al. required unchanged treatment; RESTOREX measured dose changes; Ambrogi and Mineo allowed reduction or withdrawal when symptom-free; other reports did not report changes [<citation rid="REF20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/PHM.0000000000000538" pmid="28099277" count="1">20</citation>,<citation rid="REF27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.24054" pmid="23966018" count="1">27</citation>,<citation rid="REF28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000513668" pmid="33839731" count="1">28</citation>,<citation rid="REF67" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1378/chest.128.3.1524" pmid="16162753" count="1">67</citation>,<citation rid="REF72" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/medicina58030374" pmcid="PMC8955821" pmid="35334548" count="1">72</citation>].

Rahbek et al. tested performance exactly one hour after the regular pyridostigmine dose [<citation rid="REF62" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.25552" pmid="28085204" count="1">62</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Anggarini et al. scheduled exercise 1.5-2 hours after dosing and stated that intervention and outcome measurement should occur within this peak window; actual test timing was unreported [<citation rid="REF16" ref-type="bibr" count="1">16</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Mohamed et al. began exercise 1.5-2 hours after dosing and assessed outcomes approximately three hours after ingestion, matching visits where possible [<citation rid="REF72" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/medicina58030374" pmcid="PMC8955821" pmid="35334548" count="1">72</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Andersen's journal report specified testing 0.5-2 hours after dosing; compliance was unreported [<citation rid="REF66" ref-type="bibr" count="1">66</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Wong et al. assessed anticholinesterase users approximately three hours after ingestion, whereas Ambrogi and Mineo scheduled the resistive exercise component at peak effect, usually 1.5-2 hours after dosing [<citation rid="REF20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/PHM.0000000000000538" pmid="28099277" count="1">20</citation>,<citation rid="REF27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.24054" pmid="23966018" count="1">27</citation>].

RESTOREX tested participants between 12:00 and 14:00. <sentence_start/>Eighteen participants had taken pyridostigmine six to seven hours earlier, and 20 had taken it two to three hours earlier. <sentence_start/>Timing was not associated with improvement on the 15-item Myasthenia Gravis Quality of Life Scale (MGQOL15; p = 1.00), and doses could change [<citation rid="REF28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000513668" pmid="33839731" count="1">28</citation>]. <sentence_start/>No trial randomized timing; these observations do not establish effect modification or an optimal interval.
Adherence, Tolerability, and Adverse Events

Adherence was measured inconsistently through diaries, wearable data, telephone calls, attendance, or supervised visits; other reports provided only qualitative tolerability statements. <sentence_start/>DIG-MG reported coaching attendance and ring wear, MGEX reported completed sessions, Muslihah et al. reported a mean of 23.8 of 24 sessions among 11 intervention participants, and RESTOREX reported compliance by group [<citation rid="REF28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000513668" pmid="33839731" count="1">28</citation>,<citation rid="REF40" ref-type="bibr" count="1">40</citation>,<citation rid="REF43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2021.05.002" pmid="34304969" count="1">43</citation>,<citation rid="REF61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.70234" pmid="41999078" count="1">61</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Kartika et al. reported 24 of 24 sessions for all 17 completers (nine in the intervention group and eight in the control group), but not for all randomized participants; Anggarini et al. reported attrition but not attendance at individual sessions [<citation rid="REF16" ref-type="bibr" count="1">16</citation>,<citation rid="REF42" ref-type="bibr" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These measures were not directly comparable.

Serious events were infrequent but incompletely ascertained, and minor symptoms were variably reported. <sentence_start/>Both Rahbek training groups reported transient fatigue or bulbar worsening; one participant in resistance training discontinued after substantial bulbar symptoms requiring prednisolone treatment, with causality considered possible but uncertain [<citation rid="REF62" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.25552" pmid="28085204" count="1">62</citation>]. <sentence_start/>MGEX reported no exacerbation in the exercise group and two exacerbation-related hospitalizations in the usual-care group; at least one patient-reported event occurred in 16 of 23 exercise participants and 14 of 20 usual-care participants [<citation rid="REF43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2021.05.002" pmid="34304969" count="1">43</citation>]. <sentence_start/>RESTOREX reported a crisis in the control group attributed to medication default and a renal event in the exercise group considered unrelated to exercise [<citation rid="REF28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000513668" pmid="33839731" count="1">28</citation>].

Anggarini et al. reported discomfort and intercurrent illness in the intervention group, including sinusitis, hospitalization, and a later death judged unrelated to the intervention; five of 23 randomized participants were not analysed [<citation rid="REF16" ref-type="bibr" count="1">16</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Farrugia et al. reported no clinically significant relapse, although one participant described an intersession "MG crisis"; no medical intervention or medication change occurred, and Farrugia et al. considered the episode probably a panic attack [<citation rid="REF64" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JND-170299" pmid="29889078" count="1">64</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Wong et al. reported one withdrawal related to work and one arrhythmia after intervention but before follow-up [<citation rid="REF27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.24054" pmid="23966018" count="1">27</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Reports without systematic surveillance were not treated as proof of safety.
Complete study characteristics, decisions about links between reports, medication information, adherence, withdrawals, adverse events, funding, and conflicts of interest are provided in Table 1.

Table 2 provides the 75 result-specific risk-of-bias assessments and their concise rationales. <sentence_start/>Overall RoB 2 and ROBINS-I judgments follow the rules of the respective tools. <sentence_start/>For JBI appraisals, item responses were not summed; the overall concern labels are review-specific summaries and are not official JBI scores or categories. <sentence_start/>In the 2026 JBI analytical cross-sectional tool, X1-X6 address internal validity, X7 statistical-conclusion validity, and X8 reporting; in the 2025 JBI cohort tool, C11 addresses statistical-conclusion validity.
Certainty of Evidence

Certainty was very low for every principal outcome and clinical context in Table 3. <sentence_start/>Evidence concerning habitual activity began at low certainty and was further limited by measurement and reporting problems, selection, attrition, dependence among observations, inconsistency, and uncertain direction. <sentence_start/>Intervention outcomes for function, respiration, and patient reports in stable adults were downgraded for very serious risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. <sentence_start/>Evidence for pulmonary function and walking around thymectomy was downgraded to very low because the only RCT had a high risk of bias, unreconciled inferential data, a null six-minute walk result, and an unreported outcome for hospital stay.

Evidence after hospital discharge was rated very low because the registered primary maximal inspiratory pressure (MIP) result was null, attrition was substantial, secondary reporting was selective, and several reported outcome values were internally inconsistent. <sentence_start/>Evidence after myasthenic crisis remained very low because of critical confounding and concerns about reverse causality. <sentence_start/>The body of evidence for juvenile MG was rated very low because one small active comparator trial substituted registered outcomes and reported unverifiable dispersion. <sentence_start/>Certainty about harms was also very low because surveillance was incomplete and estimates of uncommon events were imprecise.
Discussion
Principal Findings

Across selected samples, substantial proportions of participants were inactive, did not meet activity recommendations, or reported barriers to exercise, although activity distributions varied by instrument and cohort [<citation rid="REF30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JND-210637" pmid="33843693" count="1">30</citation>,<citation rid="REF31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JND-180355" pmid="30452423" count="1">31</citation>,<citation rid="REF50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2021.05.007" pmid="34303571" count="1">50</citation>-<citation rid="REF53" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/09638288.2024.2338877" pmid="38613411" count="1">53</citation>,<citation rid="REF55" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.28282" pmcid="PMC11632566" pmid="39473433" count="1">55</citation>,<citation rid="REF56" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fneur.2023.1144183" pmcid="PMC10427188" pmid="37588667" count="1">56</citation>,<citation rid="REF59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12883-025-04590-x" pmcid="PMC12822234" pmid="41408204" count="1">59</citation>,<citation rid="REF60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/22143602261463887" pmcid="PMC13439003" pmid="42348774" count="1">60</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Greater self-reported activity was associated with less fatigue or lower MG burden in several cross-sectional datasets, but reverse causality and residual confounding remain plausible; evidence from repeated measurements was sparse and heterogeneous [<citation rid="REF50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2021.05.007" pmid="34303571" count="1">50</citation>,<citation rid="REF52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JND-210722" pmid="34633330" count="1">52</citation>,<citation rid="REF55" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.28282" pmcid="PMC11632566" pmid="39473433" count="1">55</citation>,<citation rid="REF57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2021.04.002" pmid="34034925" count="1">57</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Some small intervention studies reported favourable between-group findings for selected outcomes or endpoints, as well as within-group improvements, including a binary primary outcome among participants analysed according to protocol in RESTOREX. <sentence_start/>In contrast, the primary patient-reported outcomes in DIG-MG and MGEX were null [<citation rid="REF28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000513668" pmid="33839731" count="1">28</citation>,<citation rid="REF43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2021.05.002" pmid="34304969" count="1">43</citation>,<citation rid="REF61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.70234" pmid="41999078" count="1">61</citation>].

The most defensible interpretation is that selected patients with stable, usually mild-to-moderate MG often completed individually tailored programmes. <sentence_start/>However, certainty regarding functional, respiratory, and safety outcomes was very low; the evidence does not establish a single effective prescription, population-wide safety, or a broad disease-modifying effect.

The clinical setting materially changed the interpretation of the evidence. <sentence_start/>Studies conducted around thymectomy evaluated multimodal programmes intended to preserve function during surgical recovery. <sentence_start/>The trial conducted after hospitalization evaluated inspiratory muscle training plus aerobic exercise following an exacerbation, whereas the administrative study of rehabilitation after myasthenic crisis measured billed intensity without identifying its therapeutic content [<citation rid="REF20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/PHM.0000000000000538" pmid="28099277" count="1">20</citation>,<citation rid="REF23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jns.2022.120280" pmid="35594695" count="1">23</citation>,<citation rid="REF69" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13019-023-02283-5" pmcid="PMC10127428" pmid="37095505" count="1">69</citation>-<citation rid="REF71" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12890-025-03733-7" pmcid="PMC12107784" pmid="40426137" count="1">71</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Juvenile rehabilitation addressed a separate population and used an active comparator [<citation rid="REF72" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/medicina58030374" pmcid="PMC8955821" pmid="35334548" count="1">72</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These evidence streams differed in population, comparator, additional care, outcomes, and recovery context. <sentence_start/>Combining them as equivalent evidence for chronic exercise in the community would therefore exaggerate consistency. <sentence_start/>Figure 2 summarizes the evidence contexts, exposures and interventions, mixed reported findings, and the cautious clinical interpretation supported by this heterogeneous evidence.

Comparison With Previous Reviews and Contribution of the Present Review

The 2021 focused review summarized 10 intervention studies involving 159 patients and recommended individually adapted training for mild-to-moderate MG [<citation rid="REF5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2020.12.004" pmid="33461846" count="1">5</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The 2024 scoping review included 24 interventional and observational studies involving 456 patients across varied exercise modalities and emphasized heterogeneous protocols and limited adverse event reporting [<citation rid="REF6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ctim.2024.103033" pmid="38458542" count="1">6</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The 2025 rehabilitation meta-analysis included six controlled studies [<citation rid="REF7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ensci.2025.100591" pmcid="PMC12547834" pmid="41142446" count="1">7</citation>].

The 2026 physical activity and respiratory training review included 20 studies in its qualitative synthesis and 10 in its quantitative analyses [<citation rid="REF8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-026-42949-3" pmcid="PMC13068943" pmid="41781681" count="1">8</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A separate 2026 review restricted eligibility to eight controlled adult intervention studies and used descriptive synthesis because clinical and methodological heterogeneity precluded pooling [<citation rid="REF9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/healthcare14081100" pmcid="PMC13115947" pmid="42072999" count="1">9</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Thus, eligibility criteria, included designs, and synthesis methods differed materially across prior reviews.

The present review complements rather than supersedes earlier reviews. <sentence_start/>It covers searches through July 2026 across three databases without a restriction on publication date. <sentence_start/>It integrates habitual activity, sedentary behaviour, barriers, and structured interventions. <sentence_start/>It also separates evidence from stable community populations, respiratory training, perioperative or acute recovery, and juvenile MG. <sentence_start/>Multiple publications are mapped to linked trials or cohorts, and unresolved overlap is identified.

The review also examines numerical inconsistencies; extracts disease stability, treatment, pyridostigmine timing, adherence, and adverse events; and applies risk of bias tools appropriate to each design together with certainty assessments by outcome. <sentence_start/>These procedures do not increase the certainty of the underlying evidence, but they reduce the risk of counting participants more than once or combining clinically distinct settings.
Interpretation of Efficacy and Observational Associations

For stable community-dwelling adults, activity and training should be framed as adjuncts rather than substitutes for MG-directed treatment. <sentence_start/>The null primary patient-centred outcomes in DIG-MG and MGEX show that feasibility and adherence do not guarantee clinical benefit [<citation rid="REF43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2021.05.002" pmid="34304969" count="1">43</citation>,<citation rid="REF61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.70234" pmid="41999078" count="1">61</citation>]. <sentence_start/>RESTOREX's favourable binary responder result was at high risk of bias.

Registration followed the trial; the published responder estimand was not clearly prespecified before analysis, two randomized participants were excluded, treatment changes were permitted, and responder counts in the linked report could not be reconciled [<citation rid="REF13" ref-type="bibr" count="1">13</citation>,<citation rid="REF28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000513668" pmid="33839731" count="1">28</citation>,<citation rid="REF29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12035-023-03247-5" pmid="36781738" count="1">29</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Positive secondary outcomes, uncontrolled improvements, and small-sample within-group changes should therefore be treated as hypothesis-generating.

Observational studies reported associations between activity and fatigue, disease burden, or quality of life, but they do not show that promoting activity causes these outcomes to improve [<citation rid="REF50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2021.05.007" pmid="34303571" count="1">50</citation>,<citation rid="REF52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JND-210722" pmid="34633330" count="1">52</citation>,<citation rid="REF55" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.28282" pmcid="PMC11632566" pmid="39473433" count="1">55</citation>,<citation rid="REF57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nmd.2021.04.002" pmid="34034925" count="1">57</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Qualitative and survey studies separately described barriers and facilitators, including symptoms, fear of adverse consequences, exercise knowledge, practical access, social support, and specialist supervision [<citation rid="REF53" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/09638288.2024.2338877" pmid="38613411" count="1">53</citation>,<citation rid="REF60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/22143602261463887" pmcid="PMC13439003" pmid="42348774" count="1">60</citation>].

Disease severity, depression, obesity, sleep, comorbidity, treatment, socioeconomic circumstances, and mobility can influence both activity and outcomes; higher activity may therefore partly reflect better underlying health rather than cause it. <sentence_start/>Longitudinal designs with repeated measurements should distinguish differences between participants from changes within participants. <sentence_start/>Objective monitoring should use transparent criteria for wear time and data completeness, and analyses should prespecify the time lag between activity and outcomes to strengthen causal inference.
Safety, Patient Selection, and Clinical Implications

Most community and outpatient intervention studies enrolled selected participants described as stable or well controlled and usually had mild-to-moderate generalized MG (Table 1). <sentence_start/>Stability was often incompletely operationalized, and severe or unstable disease, major bulbar or respiratory involvement, and substantial cardiopulmonary comorbidity were underrepresented. <sentence_start/>The separate trial conducted after hospital discharge was at high risk of bias [<citation rid="REF71" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12890-025-03733-7" pmcid="PMC12107784" pmid="40426137" count="1">71</citation>], and the administrative association following myasthenic crisis was at critical risk [<citation rid="REF23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jns.2022.120280" pmid="35594695" count="1">23</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These findings should not be extrapolated to recent crisis, marked bulbar or respiratory compromise, or uncontrolled comorbidity.

Reported serious events were few and often judged unrelated, but prespecified surveillance definitions and complete event reporting based on all randomized participants were usually absent. <sentence_start/>One feasibility trial reported possible training-related bulbar deterioration; the participant required prednisolone and withdrew [<citation rid="REF62" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mus.25552" pmid="28085204" count="1">62</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Incomplete and heterogeneous surveillance prevents estimation of uncommon harms or safety across the wider MG population.

The evidence does not identify a universally effective modality, intensity, frequency, duration, progression rule, or stopping threshold. <sentence_start/>If activity or exercise is considered, symptom-guided individualization and coordination with MG-directed care are prudent. <sentence_start/>These precautions derive from MG management principles and have not been validated as exercise prescriptions in trials [<citation rid="REF1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41572-019-0079-y" pmid="31048702" count="1">1</citation>,<citation rid="REF2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/WNL.0000000000011124" pmcid="PMC7884987" pmid="33144515" count="1">2</citation>].

Baseline function, current disease stability, bulbar and respiratory involvement, comorbidity, concurrent treatment and treatment changes, access, and patient preference may be relevant when tailoring activity or exercise. <sentence_start/>New or sustained weakness, dysphagia, or dyspnoea should prompt clinical reassessment. <sentence_start/>No trial randomized exercise timing relative to pyridostigmine, and reported pragmatic scheduling or exploratory observations do not establish an optimal interval.
Research Priorities

Future trials should use adequately powered, clinically characterized samples and, where sample size permits, prespecified stratification or subgroup analyses by MG phenotype and severity. <sentence_start/>Protocols should define frequency, intensity, time, type, progression, dose modification, and stopping rules; prespecify a primary estimand, clinically important thresholds, multiplicity handling, and follow-up after supervised support ends; and report concurrent medication, rescue treatment, and changes in disease state. <sentence_start/>Outcomes important to patients should distinguish MG-ADL from measures of disease status rated by clinicians, such as QMG or MGC, and should include fatigue, MG-specific quality of life, objective function, and respiratory outcomes when relevant.

Activity dose and adherence should be reported as process measures. <sentence_start/>Harms surveillance should use prespecified definitions and denominators based on all enrolled or randomized participants for symptom exacerbation, bulbar or respiratory deterioration, falls, crisis, hospitalization, treatment change or interruption, modification of the exercise dose, withdrawal, and serious and non-serious events. <sentence_start/>Registries and publications should identify linked reports and participant overlap explicitly.
Limitations

This review was not prospectively registered, and no prospectively dated protocol was available to constrain post hoc decisions. <sentence_start/>The eligibility criteria, search methods, report linkage, risk of bias assessment, and certainty framework should therefore be regarded as post hoc. <sentence_start/>The search covered PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection but did not cover Embase, the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), SPORTDiscus, the Physiotherapy Evidence Database (PEDro), or trial registries. <sentence_start/>Backward citation searching was performed, but no separate search of forward citations or grey literature was undertaken.

Restricting eligibility to full reports in English created a risk of language bias: one potentially relevant record in Chinese was excluded before retrieval, and two full reports in Russian were excluded after retrieval. <sentence_start/>One older report of ventilatory training in a mixed population with neuromuscular disease was not retrieved. <sentence_start/>The requirement that exercise-related information be a central study focus may also have omitted useful contextual evidence. <sentence_start/>The search strategy was not peer-reviewed by an information specialist, and study selection, extraction, risk of bias, and certainty judgments were not independently duplicated; these limitations increase the risks of missed studies, assessment error, and subjective judgments.

Clinical and methodological heterogeneity was substantial. <sentence_start/>Many samples were small and clinically selected. <sentence_start/>Participants were often described as stable, although stability definitions were inconsistent or absent. <sentence_start/>Evidence concerning habitual activity was predominantly cross-sectional, and several intervention reports lacked concurrent controls, robust allocation, appropriate paired or longitudinal analyses, or complete reporting based on all randomized participants.

Linkage of overlapping reports, including probable but unconfirmed overlap, required judgment and may affect assumptions about participant independence even though the count of 38 study units was retained. <sentence_start/>Numerous internal source inconsistencies could not be corrected without raw data or author clarification. <sentence_start/>Adverse events, adherence, treatment changes, and pyridostigmine timing were often incompletely reported. <sentence_start/>We therefore judged quantitative pooling inappropriate and relied on narrative synthesis. <sentence_start/>Certainty was very low across all assessed outcome and context domains.
Conclusions

In several observational datasets, greater self-reported habitual activity was associated with less fatigue, lower disease burden, or better patient-reported function, but other studies found no association. <sentence_start/>In one 12-week device cohort, only 16 of 30 enrolled participants entered the analytic sample, and no participant had complete data for all 84 days. <sentence_start/>One association within participants linked more moderate-to-vigorous physical activity with less fatigue, whereas most relationships between activity and symptoms within participants were null or inconsistent. <sentence_start/>These predominantly cross-sectional or contemporaneous associations remain vulnerable to confounding, selection, and reverse causality and do not show that increasing activity improves outcomes. <sentence_start/>For structured exercise and respiratory muscle training in selected community or outpatient adults, certainty was very low: favourable results for selected outcomes coexisted with null controlled primary outcomes, high risk of bias, imprecision, and heterogeneous interventions. <sentence_start/>It remains very uncertain whether these programmes improve objective function, respiratory performance or pulmonary function, fatigue, MG-ADL, or MG-specific quality of life.

The evidence does not establish a universal exercise prescription, population-wide safety, or the absence of uncommon clinically important harms. <sentence_start/>Evidence concerning perioperative care, recovery after crisis or hospitalization, and juvenile populations addresses distinct groups and should be interpreted within each clinical setting. <sentence_start/>Selected patients often completed prescribed programmes, but completion in small, clinically selected cohorts is not proof of efficacy or safety. <sentence_start/>If exercise is used clinically, it should remain adjunctive to MG-directed care and individualized to current disease status and comorbidity. <sentence_start/>Future studies require adequately powered and representative samples, prespecified and reproducible interventions and outcomes, transparent reporting of links between publications, appropriate longitudinal or crossover analyses, longer follow-up, and systematic reporting of adherence, treatment changes, and adverse events using all randomized participants as the denominator.
